title: Objects
summary: Objects store values under keys: how to read, change and loop over their properties.

concepts.title: Objects inside loops and arrays of objects

misconceptions.description: Believes obj.key uses the value of a variable named key, instead of reading a key literally named key.
Believes obj[name] without quotes reads a key called name, instead of using the value held in the variable name.
Believes reading a key the object lacks stops the program or gives null, instead of giving undefined.
Believes object values are read by position like array items, so reads follow the order the pairs were written.
Believes a read gives back the key name, or that a variable holds the key instead of the value stored under it.
Believes a const object cannot be changed, so assigning to its properties has no effect.
Believes assigning to an existing property combines the new value with the old one.
Believes assigning to a key the object does not have does nothing, because keys can only be set in the literal.
Believes delete only empties a value, so the key stays in the object.
Reads the value a variable has at a different moment than the one asked about, such as the end of the program.
Believes a variable copied from a property follows later changes of that property.
Believes Object.keys returns the values of the object instead of its keys.
Believes an object has a length, or that Object.keys gives a count instead of an array.
Believes the loop variable of for...of or for...in is an index number, so reading a property of it gives undefined.
Believes for...in gives the values of an object instead of its keys.
Reads a different key of the object than the one the code names, such as the id instead of the value asked for.

conceptCard.title: Objects and their properties
conceptCard.body: An object groups related values. Write it between curly braces as key: value pairs, separated by commas. Read a value with a dot and its key. A key that the object does not have gives undefined.

conceptCard.title: Dot and bracket access
conceptCard.body: Use a dot when you know the key. Use square brackets with a quoted text when the key has a space. Put a variable in the brackets to use the text it holds as the key. A dot never uses a variable.

conceptCard.title: Updating, adding and deleting properties
conceptCard.body: Assigning with = replaces a property or adds a new one. delete removes a property. The in operator checks whether a key exists. A const object can still change, because const only fixes the name.

lessons.title: Objects inside loops and arrays of objects

conceptCard.title: Objects inside loops and arrays of objects
conceptCard.body: Object.keys gives an array of an object's keys. A for...in loop visits each key in turn, and obj[key] gets its value. An array can hold objects, and for...of visits each one.

Brackets without quotes do use the variable. bin[part] reads the key ink.

hints: Compare the two reads on line 3.
A dot uses the name as written. Brackets use the value of a variable.
One read looks for part, the other looks for ink.

items.prompt: Write an expression that gives the price in prices stored under the key held in item.

A dot reads a fixed name. Brackets can use a variable.

items.prompt: Write an expression that gives the beds of the second cabin in cabins, an array of objects that each have a beds property.
items.explanation: cabins[1] is the second object, because indexes start at 0, and .beds reads its beds property. cabins[0].beds reads the first cabin, and cabins.beds looks for a property on the array itself.
hints: First pick the object from the array, then read its property.
